transcript.text: My Panasonic NN-ST45KWBPQ is sparking inside when I heat soup, little blue flashes on the right-hand wall and a crackling noise. I stopped it. Is it safe?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Stop using the microwave now: switch it off at the socket and unplug it, and don't run it again (not even empty) until we know why it sparked. Never take the outer casing off — parts inside can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged. No, it isn't safe to keep using. Stopping it was the right call. Please leave it unplugged and don't use it again until a qualified engineer has checked it, even if the sparking seems to stop. What's most likely going on: blue flashes and crackling from a spot on the right-hand wall nearly always point to the waveguide cover. That's the small flat panel (usually mica, a thin card-like material) that covers the opening where the microwaves enter the cavity. Soup is a classic trigger. Splashes dry onto that panel, the fat and salt in them absorb energy and char, and once there's a carbon mark it arcs more easily each time. In order of likelihood, the causes are:
1. Food splatter or burning on that cover panel.
2. Something metallic inside, such as a spoon, a bit of foil, or a bowl or mug with a metallic rim or pattern.
3. Chipped or burnt paint on the cavity wall leaving bare metal exposed. The magnetron itself is very rarely the cause of sparking like this. Checks you can safely do with it unplugged at the wall and the door open:
1. Look at the bowl you used and anything else that was inside. A metallic trim, foil or cutlery would explain the sparking on its own.
2. Look closely at the panel on the right-hand wall. If it's splattered but not marked, the food residue is the likely cause. If it's brown, black, bubbled or has a hole burnt in it, the cover has been damaged and will need replacing.
3. Check the paint around that area and the rest of the cavity for chips, bare metal or rust spots. Any of those would also cause arcing. You can gently wipe off any splatter with a barely damp cloth, but don't run it afterwards to see if the sparking has cleared. Tell me what you find, plus whether anything metallic was inside, and I'll tell you which cause it points to and what the engineer will likely need to do.

Thanks, I've unplugged it. No metal in there, just a plain plastic bowl with soup. The panel on the right wall has a black burnt spot on it with greasy splatter, and the paint looks fine with no chips. There was also a wisp of smoke from that spot once, which stopped when I turned it off. Does the panel need replacing?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. Probably, yes. A black burnt spot on that panel means the grease has carbonised into it, and carbon conducts. It becomes the new point the microwaves arc to, so it will keep sparking even after a clean. The smoke fits this too: it's the greasy splatter and the panel material burning at that spot. Your other findings point the same way. That leaves the cover as the clear cause, and I'm fairly confident of it. The cover isn't the whole job, though. Arcing can also mark the metal around the opening behind the panel. Occasionally it damages the magnetron's output cap, which sits behind the panel, so that needs checking too. That's why it should stay unplugged and unused until an engineer has looked at it. They'll fit a new cover and check that area at the same time. 1. Don't scrub or scrape the burnt spot. Wiping off loose grease with a barely damp cloth is fine, but you can't clean carbon out, and scraping can make it worse.
2. Have a close look at the spot. If it's only a surface mark, the damage has probably stayed in the cover. If it's burnt right through to a hole, there's a higher chance the metal behind is marked. Tell the engineer which it is. On cost: a new cover is a cheap part, so if the cavity behind is undamaged, the repair is usually well worth doing on a decent Panasonic inverter model. If the engineer finds cavity or magnetron damage, the sums change, especially on an older microwave. Is the spot just on the surface or burnt through? And roughly how old is the microwave? With those I can give you a better idea of whether repair or replacement makes more sense.

It looks like a surface burn, not a hole, as far as I can tell. The microwave is about 5 years old. I'd be happy to buy the part online and fit it myself if it's a simple clip-in one. Is that sensible?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Fitting the cover yourself isn't the sensible route here, even though the part is usually simple. On many microwaves the waveguide cover sits inside the cooking cavity and is held by clips or a small screw, so swapping it doesn't mean opening the casing. That's why it often looks like a DIY job. The difficulty is what you'd do next. After fitting it, the only way to know whether the fault is cured is to run the microwave. Because yours arced hard enough to smoke, it shouldn't be run again until a qualified engineer has checked it. 1. The metal around the waveguide opening behind the cover, for burn or pitting marks.
2. The magnetron output that sits behind the cover. A surface burn rather than a hole makes it more likely the damage stayed in the cover, but it doesn't rule out marks behind it. You can't properly judge either of those from inside the cavity. There's also the question of getting the right part. Panasonic covers vary in size, shape and fixing points, even between similar models. I can't confirm which one fits yours, so it's easy to buy the wrong one. Cutting a generic mica sheet to size is a common shortcut, but a poor fit can cause more arcing. That's normally a quick visit. Replacement would only make more sense if the engineer finds damage to the cavity or the magnetron. To stop it happening again, cover soups and sauces with a vented microwave lid. Also give the right-hand wall a quick wipe when you see splatter on it, before it gets a chance to bake on.

candidates: Food/grease splatter on, or burning of, the waveguide (mica) cover on the right-hand wall (high)
Metal in the cavity (spoon, foil, or a bowl with metallic trim) (medium)
Chipped or burnt cavity paint exposing bare metal near that spot (low)
